books.title: Steal Like an Artist
books.author: Austin Kleon
books.description: Ten short lessons on being creative in a world where everything builds on something else.
ideas: Nothing is completely original

Every creative work builds on what came before. Collect influences, study them, remix them and add your own twist. Copying one source is plagiarism; combining many and transforming them is how style is born.
steal-like-an-artist
Don't wait until you know who you are
If you waited until you fully understood yourself before making things, you'd never start. You figure out who you are by making things.
Write the book you want to read
Instead of writing what you know, make the thing you wish existed. Your taste is your guide.
Use your hands
Step away from the screen. Paper, scissors and whiteboards wake up a different part of your thinking than typing does.
Be boring
Creative work needs energy. A steady routine, enough sleep and a sensible budget give you the stability to take risks in your work.

books.title: The War of Art
books.author: Steven Pressfield
books.description: A short, punchy book about the inner force that stops us from doing our creative work.
ideas: Beat Resistance by showing up

The force that keeps you from your creative work, procrastination, self-doubt, sudden urges to do chores, is strongest right before something important. Professionals don't wait for inspiration; they sit down every day and do the work.
resistance
Resistance points to what matters
The more important a calling is to your growth, the more Resistance you'll feel toward it. Fear is a compass pointing at the work you should be doing.
Turn pro
Amateurs work when they feel like it. Professionals show up every day, no matter what, and treat creative work as a job.
The muse rewards commitment
When you commit to the work daily, help seems to appear: ideas arrive, connections form. Inspiration follows effort, not the other way round.

books.title: Big Magic
books.author: Elizabeth Gilbert
books.description: A warm, encouraging take on living a creative life beyond fear.
ideas: Let fear ride along, not drive
Fear will always come with you on creative journeys. Give it a seat in the car, but never let it pick the music or touch the steering wheel.
Ideas look for collaborators
Gilbert imagines ideas as visitors searching for someone to bring them to life. If you ignore one long enough, it may move on to someone else.
Done is better than good
Perfectionism is often fear in disguise. Finishing imperfect work teaches you more than polishing forever.
Follow curiosity, not passion
If you can't find your passion, follow small sparks of curiosity. They're easier to act on and often lead somewhere surprising.

books.title: Creativity, Inc.
books.author: Ed Catmull
books.description: Pixar's co-founder on building a culture where creative people do their best work.
ideas: Every film starts ugly
Early versions of Pixar movies were, in Catmull's words, terrible. Great work comes from protecting fragile ideas while improving them over many rounds.
The Braintrust
Pixar's directors show work in progress to a group of peers who give candid notes but have no authority. Honest feedback without power keeps it useful.
Candour is essential
If people hold back in meetings, problems stay hidden until it's too late. Leaders must make it safe to say what's not working.
Failure is part of the process
If you're not failing, you're not trying anything new. Make early mistakes cheap and fast.

books.title: The Artist's Way
books.author: Julia Cameron
books.description: A twelve-week course for recovering creative confidence.
ideas: Morning pages
Each morning, write three pages by hand of whatever comes to mind. Not art, just a brain dump. It clears mental clutter and quiets the inner critic.
The artist date
Once a week, take yourself alone on a small adventure: a museum, a market, a walk somewhere new. It refills the creative well.
Fill the well
Creativity draws on images and experiences. If you only output and never take in, you run dry.
Quiet the censor
The inner critic is loudest at the start. Treat its comments as noise, not truth, and keep going.

books.title: Show Your Work!
books.author: Austin Kleon
books.description: How sharing your process, not just finished products, helps you get discovered.
ideas: Share something small every day
Post a sketch, a note or a work-in-progress daily. Over time, these small shares add up to a body of work people can follow.
Think process, not product
Audiences love seeing how something is made. Behind-the-scenes glimpses build connection long before the final piece is ready.
Be an amateur
Amateurs share because they love the work and aren't afraid to look foolish. That openness makes them easier to relate to than experts.
Teach what you know
Explaining your methods doesn't make you replaceable. It builds trust, and people value those who share.
